 Society may be returning to business as usual, but George’s erratic behavior is freaking everyone out.
 Photo: Karolina Wojtasik/HBO 
 Sign up for The Gilded Age Club , a subscriber-exclusive newsletter where writers and editors obsess over season four.
 Society’s newfound porosity continues! Look at this dynamic season with its shifting loyalties and reconciled rivals. Now that we’ve caught up with our main characters in the first episode and moved them into their new storylines, we see even more familiar faces (*waves frantically at Mrs. Astor while she ignores me*). The rigid social guidelines have been made flexible, thanks to the constant barrage of outsiders with money and influence. Now that the gatekeepers have been unceremoniously shoved aside, our protagonists can explore new careers, venture into new parts of the city, and purchase new curtains, however hideous they may be.
 Bertha returns from England and finds Larry at home, but no George. The two men have their meeting with Rockefeller, and after a warm but cursory greeting, Larry leaves Bertha to tend to business. So Gladys is gone, Larry is pursuing his new career, and George is acting like a once-brave knight seized by a dark and terrible curse. Bertha needs a new project. Her family was furious with her for not just staying at home with them without any machinations, and now that she’s like, great, fine, I’ll stay home without any machinations, they all leave . 
 Women are making moves on Fifth Avenue and beyond. Some of these moves, like Marian’s, involve going further back into the Shame Closet. Marian is doing her excellent settlement house work, but that progressive vibe doesn’t extend to her personal life — especially when it comes to illicit storm sex with Larry. Larry tries to talk to her out on the street, and she asks if he has no shame at all about what they did. When he mentions that this is a perfect excuse to get married, Marian instead hears, “I guess I have to marry you now, uggo.” She tells him that she cannot look at him without seeing her own shame. How long, Marian, will you act like an evangelical teen?
 Her work at the settlement house is finally providing Marian a sense of purpose, as well as an avenue to practice her escapism. Why should she think about her robber-baron-in-training ex-boyfriend when she has … I don’t know, bandages to roll? I’m still not clear on what she does at the settlement house. When Ada, dressed like a curtain tassel, comes with her on a site visit, Marian tells her that the organization provides food, medical care, education, child assistance, and legal services. One of the nurses calls Marian “an asset to the program.” Later, we see her helping a boy who was burned at his job at the ironworks, but mostly the nurse helps, so is Marian there to bring in funding? I mean, that’s a helpful role. Maybe she teaches the children and then helps the nurses when they need someone to stand around.
 Agnes is furious about Marian working an evening shift on the Lower East Side. Agnes is digging her heels into the mud of tradition, glaring balefully at all who would drag her out. Ada is still refusing her more money to host the president and is instead buying the ugliest curtains; Kathy Geiss is insisting that Agnes go to the opera with a lady journalist ; Ada is going out and hiring an inept but hilarious footman; and now their niece is not only working, but working after dark. When Ada likens the work to Jesus and the lepers (they’re just poor, Ada), Agnes says, “That is all very well for Jesus; he didn’t have to make his way back to the Upper East Side.” Another classic Agnes zinger! Marian refuses to be swayed by Agnes’s opinion.
 Peggy is off on her own, which I get reflects the racially segregated social circles of the time, but I miss her interacting with the rest of the main cast. The threatening Daughters of Friendship invitation has come and been accepted, and now Peggy and Dorothy are in Newport at their initiation meeting. Everyone is in blue. Why is everyone in blue? The people in Daughters of Friendship seem like a nightmare, mainly because they have blank Stepford Wife vibes when Peggy talks about her book. One woman responds by saying her husband’s aunt put out a book of all the family recipes. See, Peggy, it’s exactly the same. Peggy then learns that Dorothy just read her novel for the first time and found it “very creative.” Devastating.
 Phylicia Rashad, a.k.a. Mrs. Kirkland, introduces Peggy and Dorothy and tells everyone that Peggy is a widow. When Dorothy and Peggy pull her to discuss this after, Mrs. Kirkland only expresses confusion. What, did they want her to tell the truth about Peggy’s background? This is Newport , not the liberal swamp of Brooklyn. This behavior on Mrs. Kirkland’s part does suck, but Peggy and William won’t be living in Newport, barring some unforeseen calamity. Something like William getting so overwhelmed by the daily insults to him as a doctor and human that he says, That’s it — we’re moving to Rhode Island. William is struggling because after he brings a long-time patient to Bellevue for an urgent procedure, the doctor there won’t let William stay. “Colored doctors are not qualified to practice at Bellevue Hospital,” he says. GTFO, sir. The other doctor, not William. You stay, William. The patient dies, and William feels powerless, an extremely justified reaction. If you’re wondering, Bellevue did not accept a Black resident until 1918 . And what the hell, let’s also mention Dr. May Edward Chinn, the first Black woman to graduate from Bellevue’s medical college in 1926. You’re so impressive, Dr. Vincent and Dr. Chinn.
 I know that you’re like, But what of the opera this season? No worries, I got you. The journalist who interviews Agnes ( BONNIE MILLIGAN, I see you ) is going to write an article about Agnes at the Met, so now Agnes has to go to the opera house that caused such a furor in previous seasons. Mrs. Astor’s opera house has quickly gone down the tubes, so there isn’t another prestigious option in town. And, fortunately for those of us who like to see a large part of the cast mingle, so many people are there!
 Mrs. Astor is in attendance, a shock. Bertha is there, wearing a dress that has been the cause of death for multiple birds. Mrs. Astor gives Bertha some advice as to absent husbands. This advice boils down to “Come up with a more believable excuse.” Carrie Astor is also at the opera, which makes me so happy, as are Enid and Oscar and Larry. The opera is a great place to pass along scuttlebutt. Enid, hoping to lord it over Bertha, tells her about Agnes hosting the president at her house and that there probably isn’t room for Bertha to come. Bertha stares, stunned. Will we get Bertha in Her Former Glory? Will this presidential dinner competition bring back her edge? Something has to happen, because I can’t handle this sad version of the Rich People Low-Key Fight Each Other show. Return to your machinations, Bertha! Steal the presidential luncheon!
 Oscar and Enid are moving forward with their salon, which I, for one, am very excited to see. Their first guest of honor is William Merritt Chase , who later founded the school that became the Parsons School of Design . This is a school so famous that I, decidedly not an Art Person, have heard of it. The Fricks are thrilled to hear about the salon, which is a real get for Oscar and Enid. What is their couple name? Encar. Osnid. Probably Osnid. Osnid continues to have the greatest potential for fun on this show, and as Senator Palpatine says, we will watch your career with great interest, Osnid. 
 Larry is lured away from whatever opera is being performed (we never learn which it is! Consider me irked!) by a friend who wants him to invest in a more entertaining medium. This medium hilariously turns out to be operetta. “No, no, no one wants that stuffy old opera business anymore. We must turn to the future and the far different operetta format.” Amazing. They’re trying to bring Gilbert and Sullivan to America — specifically, The Pirates of Penzance . I mean, that’s a good one. At least it’s not The Mikado , because then we would have to have a whole discussion about how to ethically do that show.
 And what of our curse-burdened knight? George’s Pinkerton detectives located his would-be assassin in a tenement, and we learn that it is Anne Morris’s son, Will. Do you remember Anne Morris? George Russell ruined her family in season one after her husband tried to go after George’s railroad station. Then her husband killed himself, and Anne swore revenge. Wow, Anne Morris, what a throwback. She also went to Bertha and begged her for help, and Bertha scornfully rejected her. I love a character growth moment, and we see that here through a parallel. After George and his detectives kidnap Will, Anne stops Bertha outside her house and pleads with her to intercede. This time, despite having seriously less clout in her family, Bertha listens. Anne tells her that if she loses her husband and her son, she won’t survive it. We are now encountering a Bertha who is much less assured of her place in the family, and of their own survival. Will almost killed George, and Gladys almost died in childbirth. We don’t see her agree, but she will talk to George about Will.
 George is losing it, and we get more of a window into why in his confrontation with Will. His meeting with Rockefeller goes poorly, with Rockefeller intent on gouging Russell Industries. Larry tries to be conciliatory, and George ferociously turns on him after the meeting. “You know nothing, Larry Snow,” he says. When Bertha comes to see him at his office (pre–Anne Morris encounter), she asks him to come home, telling him he looks tired. George accuses her of looking for a weakness to “lure” him back. Dude. But then, when she tries to leave, he pulls her into a makeout session that some damn assistant interrupts. Come on, man.
 When she returns the next day to discuss Will’s kidnapping, Bertha is upset that George didn’t tell her he found his attacker. George, you what? I know you’re mad at her and also everybody, but damn. Not to defend Henry Frick, but George is handling this very differently than Frick did when Sasha Berkman tried to kill him . He says if he turned Will over to the police, he would be hanged. Do you know that, sir? Berkman got 21 years in prison. George doesn’t seem moved by Bertha’s intercession.
 Later, we find where they have been keeping Will: in a room at the end of a dirty warehouse tunnel. We also find out that George is drinking laudanum . For those not in the know, laudanum is rebranded opium. It’s not great. This is not great for George. Did he get addicted to opium after his surgery, and now he’s barging around being an asshole to everyone? Maybe! Now he just has to decide whether he’s murdering Will Morris. Anne is there too for some reason. It’s really unclear why. Did he want to punish her too? Did she ferret out the location off-camera, and now they’re making her watch her son’s murder because everyone in this dirty tunnel room is terrible?
 George holds a gun to Will’s stomach, and talks about getting shot there himself, being conscious on the operating table and realizing his life was nothing. It’s really a toss-up as to whether he’ll shoot Will. I could not decide. He finally shoots off to the side, and I was like 75 percent sure he shot Anne instead, which would be fully insane. Can you imagine?! But somehow, his unfocused random shot didn’t hit any of the many people there , and Will and Anne run off, with Anne promising they’ll never set foot in New York again.
 Returning home, all the edges of George’s vision are fuzzy. That’s not great. He goes to see Bertha and tells her he let Will go. When Bertha asks him what is going on with him and their relationship, George tells her that he doesn’t know how to answer that. He has no sense of direction. Bertha needs him to make a decision, because she can’t continue in this half-life, but she wants them to be husband and wife again. Excellent. Let’s keep making these moves, show. Will George and Bertha reemerge as the power couple, or will George continue down this flushing toilet of laudanum and despair? Time will tell.
 Gossip Items for Mrs. Astor’s Next Ball 
 • Do you think if one person didn’t get the memo about wearing blue to the Daughters of Friendship meeting, they would be told to immediately leave, or just shamed into standing alone in the corner the whole time?
 • Is Ada dressing like a tassel in honor of her new curtains? Discuss.
 • Speaking of salons, has everyone seen the Renoir Sucks at Painting video that’s been circulating? It is compelling.
 ➼ How will the Russells get out of this one?
 We know you have thoughts. Comment your response below for a chance to be featured in The Gilded Age Club newsletter.
